Transcript: M: Did you like the soup at dinner? It's seaweed soup. We always have it on birthdays, so Mom made it for my sister today.
W: I liked it a lot. But why soup on a birthday?
M: My grandma says it's to thank your mother. Women eat it after they have a baby, so you eat it on the day you were born.
W: Oh, that's lovely. At home it's kind of the opposite. On your birthday, you bring a cake to school for everyone else.
M: Wait, you bring the cake? So nobody gets you one?
W: Oh, my family does, at dinner. It's just that at school it's my job. My mom always baked a honey cake, and I'd carry it in on the bus.
M: And yours is on Friday, right? Then let's stop at the bakery by the station on Friday morning. They sell big boxes of rice cakes.
W: Hmm, it doesn't feel the same if I buy it. I was thinking I could bake my mom's honey cake tomorrow night. I've got her recipe on my phone.
M: Okay, but we're out of honey. Dad finished the jar last week, putting it in his tea every morning.
W: Ah. The corner shop's open till ten, though. I could get some there.
M: Sure, but there's another thing. Ms. Lindell, our homeroom teacher, has a rule about food. Anything homemade has to be checked with her a day before.
W: A day before? So even if I bake it, I might not be allowed to share it?
M: Right. Last spring someone brought cookies with peanuts in them, and a girl in our class had to go to the nurse.
W: Oh no. My honey cake doesn't have nuts. But I guess she can't tell that just by looking at it.
M: Exactly. And bakery boxes come with a label that lists everything inside. That's why I said the bakery.
W: I see. But I still want it to be mine, you know? Something from home.
M: I get it. Could you message Ms. Lindell tonight and ask her? Then we'd know which one to do.
W: Maybe. But it's kind of late to bother a teacher. Let me think about it while I wash the dishes.
prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
choices: A school birthday custom and why the woman decides to bake a cake at home tonight
A school birthday custom and why the woman is still thinking about her cake
A school birthday custom and why the woman stops taking a cake to class
A school birthday custom and why the woman agrees to buy rice cakes at the bakery
correct_answer: A school birthday custom and why the woman is still thinking about her cake

Transcript: W: Excuse me, are you the counsellor running Saturday's orienteering race?
M: That's me. Is your cabin team signed up?
W: We are, but we've got a problem. Jolie twisted her ankle playing basketball yesterday, and the nurse says no running until next week.
M: Oh no. How's she doing?
W: She's okay, just bored. Anyway, I was thinking the three of us could race without her. We'd just carry her part of the map.
M: Hmm, the trouble is the second half. After the bridge, every team splits into two pairs, and each pair looks for different flags along the stream.
W: So with three, one of us would be out there alone.
M: Right, and we never allow that. That stretch is easy to get lost in. I put the flags out this morning, and even I took a wrong turn.
W: Couldn't the three of us just stay together the whole time?
M: Then you'd have to find every flag on both routes. You'd still be in the woods when the dinner bell rings.
W: Oh. I didn't think of that.
M: Okay, here's one idea. Borrow someone. The Kanby cabin has five campers this year, so one of them hasn't got a team for Saturday.
W: I'd rather not. I know it's allowed, and I don't mind someone new. But Jolie practised with her compass every single evening. If somebody else just takes her place, all that work was for nothing.
M: Fair enough. Then what if she doesn't lose her place? Every team checks in by radio with the start tent. Usually a counsellor takes the calls, but Jolie could do it for you. She'd sit with me, keep the big map, and talk you through it if you get stuck by the stream. The Kanby camper would just run as your fourth, and the results would still list Jolie.
W: Oh, she'd love that. She's always telling us which way to go anyway.
M: Great, that solves two problems at once. Just check with the Kanby counsellor first. She's down at the lake until four. And remember, nobody sees the race map until the start on Saturday.
W: It's only two now, so I'll go and tell Jolie first. She's resting in our cabin.
M: Good. Tell her to bring a hat. It gets hot in that tent.
prompt: According to the woman, how did Jolie hurt her ankle?
choices: She twisted it playing basketball.
She slipped on a wet rock by the stream.
She tripped on the dock at the lake.
She fell down the cabin steps.
correct_answer: She twisted it playing basketball.

Transcript: W: Thanks for giving up your lunch, Emil. So, everyone's talking about the time capsule. How did you find it?
M: Honestly, it was luck. I was looking through old yearbooks in the library for my history project, and in the one from nineteen ninety-nine there's a photo of some students burying a metal box.
W: And the photo didn't say where?
M: The caption just said behind the old gym. But the old gym was knocked down years ago, so that didn't help much.
W: Then how did you work out the spot?
M: There's a huge oak tree in the background of the photo, with one branch that bends right down. That tree's still standing next to the bike shed. So I lined up the photo with the tree, and I was pretty sure the box was under the shed.
W: That's really clever. Who did the digging?
M: The caretaker did most of it. We started straight after the last bell, at half past three. He had to move two bikes and a pile of bricks first. When the shovel finally hit metal, it was half past five, and he'd missed his bus home.
W: Oh no. So what's the box like?
M: Smaller than I expected, about the size of a shoebox. It's rusty along one side, though, so I'm worried rainwater got in and spoiled some of the papers.
W: Okay. Now, about the article itself.
M: Actually, I was going to ask. Could you hold it until after the box is opened? Then you could write about what's inside and have photos of everything.
W: When's it being opened?
M: At the spring concert, in three weeks. The head teacher wants to do it on stage.
W: I see why you'd want to wait. But I've got another idea. What if we run a short story this Friday and ask anyone from the class of nineteen ninety-nine to come to the concert? The people who buried it could explain the things inside.
M: Hmm. But some of them must live far away by now.
W: Some, maybe. But lots of parents here went to this school. Somebody will know somebody. And after the concert, I'll write a second, longer piece with the photos.
M: Okay, that's actually better than my plan. Two articles, then.
W: Great. Thanks, Emil. I'll show you the first one before it goes in.
prompt: What can be inferred about the search the man describes?
choices: It took about four hours.
It took about two hours.
It took about three hours.
It took about eight hours.
correct_answer: It took about two hours.

W: No bikes today. The man who fixes them is away, so just tell people to come back on the fourteenth.

Transcript: W: Excuse me, Mr. Gaddis? Have you got a minute?
M: Sure. What's up?
W: I want to start walking people's dogs, here in the building. I'm saving for a drawing course this summer. But I don't know how to let people know.
M: Put a few lines in the building newsletter. It goes into everyone's mailbox on Friday, and I'm the one who puts it together.
W: The newsletter? Does anyone actually read that? I thought I'd just put a sign on the board by the mailboxes.
M: Nobody looks at that board. It's covered in old takeaway menus. But the newsletter gets read, especially by the older residents. Mrs. Gantry on the third floor reads every word, and she's got two dogs and bad knees.
W: Hmm. What about flyers? I could print some and slide them under everyone's door tonight.
M: I wouldn't. A pizza place did that last spring, and so many people complained that the residents voted to ban it. You'd get a warning letter before your first walk.
W: Oh, I didn't know that. Okay, the newsletter, then. What should I write?
M: Just your name, your flat number and what you charge. Get it to me by Wednesday night.
W: I was thinking five dollars for half an hour. Is that too much?
M: No, that's fair. Actually, could you start with Huxley? My knee's been bad since I slipped on the ice in January, and he hasn't had a proper walk in weeks.
W: Your beagle? Of course! When would you want me?
M: Mornings, if you can. Around seven, before school. Could you start on Monday?
W: Monday's fine. But I've got swim practice at half past six on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so on those days I'd have to come after dinner instead.
M: That's no problem. He'll be happy to get out at any time. Want to come up and meet him now? He's a bit shy with new people.
W: Sure. Let me just drop my school bag at home first. I'll knock on your door in five minutes.
M: Great. I'll put the kettle on.
prompt: What will the woman probably do right after the conversation?
choices: Take the man's beagle out for its first walk
Go upstairs with the man right away to meet his shy beagle
Drop her school bag at home and then knock on the man's door
Print some flyers to slide under the neighbours' doors
correct_answer: Drop her school bag at home and then knock on the man's door
